A historic drop for Alphabet's stock dragged the U.S. stock market lower.

The S&P 500 fell 0.3% Thursday, its first drop in four days. The loss came even though the majority of stocks within the index and across Wall Street rose. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%.

Google's parent company was the main reason for the losses, and had its worst drop on record after reporting weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The report underscored worries about whether huge investments in AI will pay off. Treasury yields fell.

On Thursday:

The S&P 500 fell 23.59 points, or 0.3%, to 7,720.39.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 132.54 points, or 0.3%, to 52,342.56.

The Nasdaq composite fell 365.13 points, or 1.4%, to 26,184.72.

The Russell 2000 rose 28.71 points, or 1%, to 2,859.22.

detail:
Why These 3 ETFs Are a Gentle First Step for a 66-Year-Old Who Owns Nothing but Bonds

Quick Read

AOM holds roughly 60% bonds and 40% stocks in one ticker, giving a bond-heavy investor global diversification with modest equity exposure.

SPHQ screens S&P 500 companies for high return on equity, low debt, and cash-backed earnings at a 0.15% expense ratio.

FVD uses near-equal weighting of roughly 0.4% per position, preventing any single dividend payer from dominating the $8 billion fund.

You're 66, and every dollar you've saved sits in bonds. Maybe you moved there after a bad market shook you. Maybe stocks never felt comfortable. Either way, you built something stable, and that took discipline. The question now is whether that portfolio fits a retirement that could last decades. If you decide to add some stock exposure, three funds offer a measured way in: iShares Core 40/60 Moderate Allocation ETF (NYSEARCA:AOM), Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF (NYSEARCA:SPHQ), and First Trust Value Line Dividend Index Fund (NYSEARCA:FVD).

PeopleImages / Shutterstock.com
Why an All-Bond Portfolio Can Quietly Fall Short

For some retirees, an all-bond portfolio makes sense. If Social Security, a pension, or an annuity already covers your spending, you may not need more growth. Bonds also pay real income today, with the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.00% as of Oct. 26. However, bond funds can still lose value, especially when rates climb.

For everyone else, the risk is quieter than a crash. Over a long retirement, inflation and longevity can slowly eat away at a portfolio that never grows much. Stocks give you a claim on corporate earnings growth, something a fixed coupon can't provide.

------

The Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now

------

Owning stocks comes with a price. Part of your portfolio will now decline sometimes, occasionally sharply. Go in expecting that, and remember that a rough market in the first few years of retirement does far more lasting damage than one later on (we walked through that sequence-of-returns problem, and how to defend against it, in a free guide here).

How to Start Small and Avoid a Surprise Tax Bill

There's no need to move a lot or move it all at once. Shift a modest portion, add to it gradually, and see how the swings feel before going further.

Where your bonds live matters. According to the IRS, "Generally, amounts in your IRA, including earnings and gains, aren't taxed until distributed" (Publication 554). This generally allows you to shift bond holdings inside an IRA without triggering a tax bill at the time of the trade. In a taxable account, selling bonds can realize a gain or a loss, so check before you sell.

AOM Adds Stocks While Bonds Stay in Charge

AOM is the easiest step because it adds stocks inside a fund that still holds plenty of bonds. Its name signals a 40/60 stock-to-bond mix. As of July 31, 2026, its largest position was a U.S. bond index fund at about 49.6% of net assets, plus an international bond fund at roughly 8.9%. On the stock side, an S&P 500 index fund made up about 23.4%, with international developed markets at 11.7% and emerging markets at 4.4%.

One ticker gets you global diversification and automatic rebalancing. The fund holds roughly $1.74 billion in net assets and pays quarterly, distributing about $1.55 per share over the trailing 12 months. Payouts vary from quarter to quarter.

SPHQ Screens for Financially Sturdy Companies

SPHQ tracks the S&P 500 Quality Index, a subset of S&P 500 companies "determined to have high quality based on return on equity, accruals ratio, and financial leverage ratio." Translated: profitable businesses whose earnings are backed by cash, carrying manageable debt.

It costs a 0.15% net expense ratio, has operated since Dec. 6, 2005, and manages about $19.4 billion. No single holding topped roughly 5.8% of assets as of July 31, and exposure covers technology, financials, industrials, consumer brands, and health care. It paid about $0.87 per share in quarterly dividends over the past year.

Quality screens don't prevent declines. SPHQ slipped 0.91% over the past month alone.

FVD Pays Quarterly Income From Safety-Ranked Dividend Stocks

FVD tracks the Value Line Dividend Index, which selects dividend payers that Value Line ranks for safety and that yield more than the S&P 500. The index uses modified equal dollar weighting, so positions sat near 0.4% each as of June 30, 2026. No single company dominates.

You get utilities, insurers, health care, consumer staples, and real estate trusts, plus some international names. The fund holds about $8.04 billion and distributed $1.1225 per share over the trailing 12 months, most recently $0.2562 paid on Sept. 30. Companies can cut dividends, and FVD remains a stock fund that can fall with the market.

Trade-Offs to Weigh Before You Commit

Each fund asks you to accept something. AOM's bond-heavy mix moderates both the swings and the growth, and it can still decline. SPHQ leans heavily on chipmakers and tech names, which can be volatile. FVD's tilt toward utilities and real estate trusts can lag if rates climb.

Used gradually, these funds let you test stock ownership on your terms: one blended fund that keeps bonds in charge, one that screens for financial strength, and one built around steady dividend payers. For a 66-year-old who owns nothing but bonds, that combination offers a way to add growth potential without giving up the stability you worked to build.

detail:

stocks market trading wall street equity -Shutterstock

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 fell Thursday, snapping a three-day advance, following a disappointing earnings report from Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) and hot inflation data.

The Nasdaq shed 1.4% to close at 26,184.72. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.3% each to 7,720.39 and 52,342.56. respectively. Among sectors, communication services saw the steepest decline of 6.6%, while healthcare paced the gainers.

Alphabet's class A and C shares both tumbled nearly 13%, among the steepest declines on the S&P 500. It class A shares were worst the performer on the Dow. The company's third-quarter results missed Wall Street's estimates despite artificial intelligence-led cloud revenue growth as capital expenditure more than doubled annually.

Alphabet's Google search revenue miss drove the third-quarter top-line shortfall as more people used AI-powered summaries that appear at the top of search results, BofA Securities said in a note Thursday.

Caterpillar followed Alphabet on the Dow, down 9.3%. Its third-quarter revenue missed Wall Street's estimates, while the company said it expects "moderate" sales growth in the ongoing quarter.

Microsoft edged down 0.2%, trimming its losses for the day following the release of its fiscal first-quarter results late Wednesday. The software giant's strong balance sheet and cash flow position it to sustain elevated AI infrastructure spending without compromising its financial position as investors increasingly scrutinize returns on AI investments, Truist Securities said in a client note.

In other company news, DoorDash (DASH) agreed to acquire Maplebear (CART), which does business as Instacart, in a roughly $17 billion deal aimed at strengthening their grocery delivery business, while the food delivery company reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results.

DoorDash jumped 5.6%, while Maplebear fell 2.2%.

In economic news, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge accelerated in September, government data showed, increasing the odds of a rate hike by the end of the year. The headline personal consumption expenditure price index rose 3.6% year over year, while the core measure, which excludes food and energy, increased to 3.1%, from 3.4% and 3% in August, respectively.

"Alongside firm economic activity, this renewed inflation momentum keeps another Fed rate hike in December firmly on the table," TD Economics said.

The US economy expanded at the fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, aided by robust consumer spending, official data showed Thursday.

The Fed held its policy rate steady on Wednesday in a divided decision as the central bank preferred to wait for fresh data before deciding its next move. Chair Kevin Warsh announced a reduction in the number of rate-setting meetings from the current eight annually to devote more time to monetary policy strategy discussions.

Treasury yields were lower, with the two-year rate retreating 12.9 basis points to 4.61% and the 10-year rate off 10.4 basis points to 4.94%.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil fell 0.1% to $102.71 a barrel in Thursday late-afternoon trade, while Brent edged up 0.2% to $115.58 a barrel.

US Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to the secretary of Iran's supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, at the direction of President Donald Trump, to resume peace negotiations, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.

Qatar has presented Iran a new proposal to end the Middle East war, but a senior Iranian official rejected the offer as unacceptable, Reuters reported.

Spot gold dipped 1% to $4,028.41 per troy ounce, while silver lost 2.4% to $52.36 per ounce.

LPL Financial (LPLA) stock fell 15.2% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, as the S&P 500 gained 0.3%. The selloff followed the company's October 27 release of its third-quarter results and an update on Commonwealth Financial Network, whose advisers LPL plans to bring onto its platform in mid-November. What did LPL report, and what changed in its plans for Commonwealth?

LPL Reported Results And Expects Lower Commonwealth Retention

LPL posted adjusted third-quarter earnings of $5.97 per share, topping the $5.66 analysts had estimated. While revenue of $5.34 billion came in just under the $5.35 billion estimate, management called the adjusted earnings figure a record.

The company also updated its outlook for Commonwealth. Management now expects to keep about 83% of Commonwealth's assets when the advisers move over. A quarter earlier, management said the figure stood at around 85% for advisers who had signed, down from the 90% LPL planned on when it first assessed the deal. Management said the lower figure came from a small number of advisers who signed but did not stay.

Based on that retention and current market levels, LPL estimates Commonwealth will bring in about $415 million a year in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization once it is fully integrated. Management expects to reach that rate by the fourth quarter of 2027.

Recruiting also slowed from the prior year. Advisers who joined LPL in the quarter brought $24 billion in assets, down 26% from a year ago.

Financial Stocks Rose As LPL Fell

The selloff was specific to LPL. Financial stocks advanced as a group during the session, with XLF, the fund that tracks the sector, up 0.4%. LPL's peers moved far less, with Raymond James Financial falling 0.4% and Morgan Stanley rising 1.7%.

Shares Of LPL Closed Near A One-Year Low

LPL had not suffered a single-session drop of this size at any point in the prior 365 days. The stock finished at $269.19, resting just above its lowest close of the past year, $265.86 on May 28, 2026. The highest close in that period was $393.25 on February 9, 2026.

Over the past year, LPL stock lost 21.3%, while the S&P 500 returned 14.0%. Most of that decline materialized recently, with the shares losing 20.6% in the three months to October 28 against a 4.4% gain for the index.

LPL's next report will cover the fourth quarter of 2026, the period in which it plans to complete the Commonwealth conversion. The share of Commonwealth's assets that LPL keeps after the conversion is the measure to watch in that report.

title: Stocks Break Winning Streak Dragged by Alphabet's Worst Ever Post-Earnings Performance
detail:
Stocks Break Winning Streak Dragged by Alphabet's Worst Ever Post-Earnings Performance

^IXIC

Trading disclosure

Stocks fell on Thursday, breaking a three-day winning streak and dragged by Alphabet, which recorded its worst post-earning slump since going public more than 20 years ago after dropping more than 12%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.29%, while the S&P 500 did so 0.32%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite, where Alphabet has a larger representation, plummeted 1.40%.

Alphabet wiped out some $500 billion in market value after reporting a larger negative free cash flow than analysts had expected. The figure stood at $9.07 billion for the third quarters, much higher than the $2.70 billion expected by analysts. The company kept its capital expenditures guidance for the next year unchanged: between $195 billion and $205 billion.

The company is facing challenges from the rise of AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic as their models take their queries outside Google. Gemini, the company's chatbot, has not been keeping up with ChatGPT and Claude.

Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the company's search business has been taking hits from lower monetization within the AI mode. He went on to say that Alphabet is "scaling" ads within the AI overviews and AI Mode products.

Elsewhere, odds of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve in December decreased slightly on Thursday after September's inflation rate was in line with expectations and the GDP grew at a robust pace, but still remains elevated.

Chances of a hike stood at 79.6% on Thursday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. That stands in contrast with 84.2% from Wednesday, before the latest figures were released.

The personal consumption expenditures price index climbed a seasonally adjusted 0.5% last month. The annual rate stood at 3.6%, slightly below the Dow Jones consensus but well above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal.

The core PCE index, which excludes food an energy, gained 0.3% for the month and 3.1% for the year, in line with the consensus.

In the geopolitical area, Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to the Iranian leadership emphasizing that any path towards a new deal must include "discussions on the nuclear issue."

The letter in question was sent to top Iranian military leader Mohsen Rezaei, who has a direct line to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. "The President was enthusiastic about the letter," a U.S. official told Axios.

The development comes after another report noted that Iranian leaders will take a proposal detailing nuclear concessions to the U.S. in exchange for sanctions relief to avoid a return to a full-fledged war to Khamenei.

However, at the same time Trump received a rare in-person briefing on military options for Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal. The president has repeatedly floated the possibility of returning to full-fledged hostilities after the midterm elections.
